title: Haemorrhagic shock
subtitle: Recognise, stop the bleeding, resuscitate

sources.org: American College of Surgeons Committee on Trauma
sources.title: Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) Student Course Manual

sources.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
sources.title: Major trauma: assessment and initial management (NG39)

red_flags.text: A narrowing pulse pressure with a rising heart rate. This precedes any fall in systolic pressure.
Transient responder: pressure improves with the first unit and falls again. That patient is still bleeding.
Base deficit worse than -6, or a lactate above 4 mmol/L, in a patient who looks compensated.
Agitation or confusion attributed to alcohol or pain. In a bleeding patient it is cerebral hypoperfusion until proven otherwise.
A young or pregnant patient with normal observations and a serious mechanism. They compensate until they do not.

do_now.text: Compress or clamp what you can see. External haemorrhage is the one cause you can treat with your hands.
Two large-bore cannulae, bloods, crossmatch, and activate the major haemorrhage protocol before you are certain you need it.
Give blood, not crystalloid, once haemorrhagic shock is recognised.
Tranexamic acid early in traumatic haemorrhage.

assess.text: Find the source: chest, abdomen, pelvis, long bones, external, and in the post-operative patient the operative field.
Classify the response to the first transfusion - responder, transient responder, non-responder. That classification is the decision.
Look for the confounders: beta-blockade blunts tachycardia, a pacemaker fixes the rate, and pregnancy raises baseline volume.
Estimate allowable loss and transfusion need rather than guessing.

investigate.text: Serial venous or arterial gas: lactate and base deficit track resuscitation better than blood pressure.
Haemoglobin early is reassuringly normal in acute loss and must not be used to exclude bleeding.
Coagulation screen, fibrinogen, ionised calcium and platelets, repeated during massive transfusion.
Point-of-care viscoelastic testing where available, to direct component therapy rather than fixed ratios.
Imaging only when it changes the destination. A non-responder's investigation is a laparotomy.

resuscitate.text: Balanced component therapy in massive haemorrhage: red cells with plasma and platelets rather than red cells alone.
Replace calcium during massive transfusion. Citrate chelates it and hypocalcaemia worsens both coagulopathy and cardiac output.
Permissive hypotension until haemorrhage is controlled, in the absence of significant head injury. Aim for a radial pulse and a talking patient rather than a number.
Actively rewarm. Hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy reinforce each other and the only one you fully control is temperature.
Vasopressors do not treat an empty tank and mask the loss. Reserve them for the resuscitated patient with vasoplegia.

definitive.text: Definitive treatment is surgical or radiological control of the bleeding point. Everything else buys time for it.
Damage control laparotomy for the exhausted patient: pack, control contamination, temporary closure, intensive care, planned return.
In the post-operative patient, re-exploration is the answer far more often than another unit of blood.

escalate.text: Consultant surgeon, consultant anaesthetist, interventional radiology and the blood bank, simultaneously and early.
Critical care must know at the point the major haemorrhage protocol is activated, not when the operation ends.
Transfer only after haemorrhage is controlled, unless the receiving unit is the only place control is possible - and then go with blood running.

notes: Blood pressure is the last thing to fall and the first thing everyone watches.
The commonest error is repeated crystalloid: it raises pressure, displaces clot, dilutes factors and cools the patient.
Every number in this protocol supports a decision that is fundamentally binary - is the bleeding controlled or not.
